Added weapons and the possibility of Jordyn Tyson returning healthy create a route to stronger second-half production, with multiple evaluations placing his upside around the QB1 fringe.

The main concern is that touchdown growth is still an assumption rather than an established expectation. Early-season receiving health could cap his ceiling, especially if Tyson is unavailable, and the offense must convert more opportunities for the breakout case to fully materialize. A middle-tier offensive line and neutral quarterback schedule do not materially change the outlook. At roughly QB20-QB21, Shough is a worthwhile late redraft selection who offers meaningful upside without requiring an early investment.
summaries.pros_summary: Rushing and goal-line ability, late-season receiving upside, and a QB20 price create worthwhile sleeper value.
summaries.cons_summary: Touchdown growth is unproven, early receiving health is uncertain, and the ceiling depends on Tyson returning healthy.

summaries.card_summary: Tyler Warren is a reasonable target at a non-premium price, with a second-year breakout path built on 112 rookie targets and a strong offensive line. The case is highly sensitive to sophomore development, touchdown growth, and his groin injury remaining short-term; a premium price near TE4 value leaves little margin for error.
summaries.full_writeup:
Warren has a credible sophomore-jump case after seeing 112 targets as a rookie, and his surrounding offensive line ranks among the league’s strongest in preseason evaluation. That combination supports improved efficiency and a path toward the upper tier of tight ends, especially if his current market cost remains below comparable breakout candidates. The neutral schedule is mostly a tiebreaker rather than a meaningful projection input.

The opposing case is that rookie volume did not translate into elite efficiency or reliable touchdown access, making a premium selection difficult to justify without clear year-two growth. His groin injury was keeping him out of practice as of August 26, though Week 1 was not considered in danger if he returned the following week; any setback would materially alter the outlook. Warren is best treated as a price-sensitive target rather than an automatic early tight-end selection, with PPR formats offering the clearest support.
summaries.pros_summary: 112 rookie targets, a strong offensive line, and a credible sophomore breakout path support the upside.
summaries.cons_summary: Rookie efficiency and touchdown access were modest, groin uncertainty persists, and TE4 pricing leaves little margin.

summaries.card_summary: Tyrone Tracy Jr. is a useful late-round contingency back with receiving value and RB2 upside if Cam Skattebo misses time. A healthy Skattebo likely limits Tracy to a complementary role, while a weak offensive line makes his standalone floor less secure despite a favorable schedule.
summaries.full_writeup:
Tracy profiles as a worthwhile late bench investment because his receiving ability can provide value even without full control of the backfield, and his ceiling rises sharply if Cam Skattebo is unavailable. His 48 targets in 2025 provide some support for that pass-game path, while the favorable running-back schedule is a modest additional positive. At a pick around 128, the contingency upside is more appealing than his current RB53 market range might imply.

The central problem is playing time. A healthy Skattebo is expected to control much of the early-down work, which can leave Tracy dependent on passing situations or an injury ahead of him. The team’s weak preseason offensive-line ranking also limits confidence in efficient rushing production. Tracy is a stronger PPR bench target than a player to rely on as a weekly starter from the outset, with his value tied to role clarity and Skattebo’s health.
summaries.pros_summary: Receiving value, RB2 contingency upside, and a favorable schedule make a late bench pick attractive.
summaries.cons_summary: A healthy Skattebo likely controls early downs, the offensive line is weak, and standalone weekly reliability is limited.

summaries.card_summary: Wan'Dale Robinson is a strong late-round PPR target after consecutive 140-target seasons and continuity in Brian Daboll’s system. His floor depends on another heavy short-area role, while Carnell Tate and Calvin Ridley, an uncertain team passing ceiling, and a weak offensive line create meaningful downside.
summaries.full_writeup:
Robinson’s appeal is volume. He enters 2026 after consecutive seasons with roughly 140 targets and familiarity with Brian Daboll’s system, giving him a plausible path to remain a high-percentage, short-area option. That profile is particularly attractive in PPR formats when he is priced around WR39-48 or in Rounds 9-10, and it can outweigh concerns about his lack of explosive-play upside. The neutral schedule neither strengthens nor weakens the case materially.

The outlook is less secure than the target history alone suggests. Carnell Tate and Calvin Ridley create legitimate competition, and Tennessee’s overall passing output is uncertain. A preseason offensive-line ranking near the bottom of the league could further pressure the offense and limit efficiency, even if Robinson retains a substantial share of the work. He is a volume-based value target, with the best return coming in PPR leagues and at a price that does not assume another 140-target season.
summaries.pros_summary: Consecutive 140-target seasons, system continuity, and a late PPR price provide a strong volume-based floor.
summaries.cons_summary: Tate and Ridley threaten target share, the passing ceiling is uncertain, and a weak offensive line limits efficiency.

summaries.card_summary: Woody Marks is an appealing late handcuff with receiving-work upside and a possible split role behind David Montgomery. Montgomery remains favored for early downs and goal-line touches, while a weak offensive line makes Marks more dependent on passing volume or an injury-driven promotion.
summaries.full_writeup:
Marks offers useful contingency value at a late price, particularly because he is reportedly earning third-down and receiving work in a backfield that could be closer to a split than his cost implies. His 36 targets in 2025 give the receiving role some historical basis, and the favorable running-back schedule is a modest plus. If David Montgomery misses time, Marks has a credible path to RB2 production rather than merely being a deep reserve.

The standalone outlook remains constrained by role. Montgomery is still expected to control early-down and goal-line opportunities, which limits Marks’ touchdown and rushing volume unless the split expands. The team’s weak preseason offensive-line ranking also lowers confidence in efficient rushing production. Marks is best drafted as a late PPR-oriented contingency piece around the stated ADP near 178, not as a player whose current role should be treated as a stable weekly workload.
summaries.pros_summary: Third-down receiving work, favorable contingency upside, and a late price create useful PPR appeal.
summaries.cons_summary: Montgomery remains favored for early downs and goal-line work, while a weak offensive line limits standalone rushing value.

summaries.card_summary: Xavier Worthy is a speculative post-hype sleeper whose reduced cost could capture a rebound from a talented receiver. The case is thin and depends on a larger role than his 73-target 2025 season, with a difficult schedule and uncertain target distribution limiting confidence.
summaries.full_writeup:
Worthy has a plausible rebound profile if outside circumstances depressed his 2025 production and his role expands in 2026. The offense’s preseason offensive-line ranking is strong, and the team directed 56.9% of its targets to wide receivers last season, providing a generally favorable structural backdrop. At a WR47 market range, he can be considered when drafting for upside rather than immediate certainty.

Still, the player-specific case is not robust enough to treat him as a priority target. Worthy had only 73 targets last season, and the available outlook offers limited detail on how his usage will materially change. The difficult preseason receiver schedule is a modest negative, though it should not drive the decision. Worthy is best viewed as a price-sensitive late sleeper whose return depends on earning more consistent volume; he carries considerably more volatility than a receiver with an established target floor.
summaries.pros_summary: Post-hype rebound potential, a strong offensive line, and a WR47 price offer speculative upside.
summaries.cons_summary: Only 73 targets provide limited volume certainty, target distribution is unclear, and the difficult schedule adds volatility.

summaries.card_summary: Charbonnet is a late-round touchdown and committee upside play if he returns healthy, with a favorable 2026 RB schedule as a minor boost. The key risk is his ACL recovery, which could keep him out until October and erase much of his early-season value.
summaries.full_writeup:
Charbonnet profiles as a speculative depth pick whose fantasy value would come from committee work and goal-line opportunities rather than a clear every-down role. His 2025 usage was modest at 24 targets, while a middle-tier offensive line does little to materially change that outlook. A favorable preseason RB schedule is a small positive tiebreaker, not a reason to aggressively pursue him.

The outlook is highly sensitive to his rehabilitation timeline. If he is available early enough to establish a role, his touchdown potential could make him useful in non-PPR formats; if the ACL recovery extends into October, his market-level RB47 valuation becomes much harder to justify. Treat him as a conditional late-round bench option rather than a dependable weekly starter.
summaries.pros_summary: Committee and goal-line upside, favorable schedule, and late-round bench appeal if ACL recovery permits an early return.
summaries.cons_summary: ACL recovery could extend into October, his receiving role is limited, and committee usage offers little weekly security.

summaries.card_summary: Branch is a better dynasty stash than 2026 redraft target, with explosive playmaking that could earn designed touches over time. His immediate role, health, team context, and draft price remain unsettled, reflected by a much stronger dynasty outlook than his WR82 non-PPR market rank.
summaries.full_writeup:
Branch has intriguing dynasty upside because his playmaking could translate into manufactured touches and a larger offensive role. The team’s strong preseason offensive-line ranking and 2025 wide-receiver target share provide a reasonable environment for young pass catchers, though neither guarantees Branch meaningful snaps in 2026. A neutral WR schedule is largely irrelevant compared with his role development.

The formats point in different directions: he is valued as a tier-4 dynasty rookie and a potential long-term stash, but his current non-PPR redraft standing is much lower. That makes him difficult to treat as a dependable 2026 contributor. He fits best on dynasty benches or in deep leagues where managers can absorb uncertain early usage and wait for the designed-touch role to materialize.
summaries.pros_summary: Explosive playmaking, designed-touch upside, and a strong offensive environment make him an intriguing dynasty stash.
summaries.cons_summary: Immediate snaps, health, and team context remain uncertain, while his WR82 redraft price offers little 2026 reliability.

summaries.card_summary: Flowers carries legitimate WR1 breakout upside in PPR formats, supported by strong efficiency and possible touchdown growth, with a favorable schedule as a modest plus. His price already reflects a high-end expectation, and his dated late-August ankle issue plus a weak offensive line add meaningful risk.
summaries.full_writeup:
Flowers has the clearest ceiling of this group, with elite yards-per-route-run production and room for touchdown growth to push him into the true WR1 tier. His 2025 workload—118 targets—supports a substantial role, while the favorable preseason WR schedule offers a small additional positive. The case is strongest in PPR, where volume and receiving efficiency are more valuable.

The main concern is that improved scoring and consistent weekly output are required to outperform a current WR14 non-PPR market valuation. The offensive line ranks in the weak tier, which could pressure the passing environment, and Flowers missed practice Monday and Wednesday as of August 26 after apparently tweaking his ankle the prior week. That injury news is dated and should not be treated as a current diagnosis, but it reinforces the need to confirm his health before paying a premium.
summaries.pros_summary: Elite route efficiency, substantial target volume, and touchdown growth create legitimate PPR WR1 upside.
summaries.cons_summary: Premium WR14 pricing demands improved scoring, while a weak offensive line and dated ankle issue add risk.
